newsitem.title: UK: EBRD urged to get tough on nuclear safety.
newsitem.headline: EBRD urged to get tough on nuclear safety.

text.p: Environmental groups on Tuesday urged the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and other major lending agencies to take a tough stance on countries accused of dragging their feet on nuclear safety.
The CEE Bankwatch Network, representing environmentalists from 13 countries, told a news conference that future loans should be linked to plant closure commitments being respected.

"Once a closure date has been agreed to, all future energy loans made by international financial institutions should be tied to the closure of these unacceptably dangerous facilities," it said in a statement.

Yuri Urbansky of the National Ecological Centre of Ukraine accused the Kiev government of blackmailing the West over closure of the Chernobyl power station, responsible for the world's worst nuclear accident in 1986.

Ukraine says it is meeting its obligations under a memorandum of understanding in 1995 with the Group of Seven leading industrial nations, calling for closure of Chernobyl by 2000 in exchange for $2.3 billion of financing.
That sum, which Ukraine says it needs to cover the cost of closing the plant and building up alternative energy supplies, has since swollen to over $3 billion.

Urbansky criticised the Ukrainian government for supporting completion of two unfinished Soviet-designed nuclear plants -- Khmelnitsky 2 and Rovno 4 (K2/R4) -- instead of exploiting alternative non-nuclear energy sources.
"We will just get two new unsafe nuclear reactors," he said.

The environmentalists appealed to the EBRD on the fringes of its annual meeting to reject a loan for the K2/R4 plants which the bank has been considering. An independent panel has concluded that this might not be the best use of funds earmarked to improve nuclear safety.
"The K2/R4 project is a vital test of the EBRD's environmental and democratic credibility," Urbansky said.
The EBRD manages a Nuclear Safety Account (NSA), which is financed by 15 countries to help close high risk reactors.
The fund has so far given five grants totalling 250 million ecus to four countries, but no reactors have been closed.
The CEE Bankwatch Network said the NSA should not be extended unless it specified closure dates.
